To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) transfer learning of feature representations and classifiers can be successfully performed across heterogeneous robots, 2) the transfer of feature representations can result in a larger reduction in error than transfer of classifiers alone, 3) alignment of learned feature representations across robots can further improve the transfer of classifiers, 4) the alignment procedure can be successfully applied to heterogeneous robots using different cameras, and 5) the Fisher vector encoding method results in the smallest reduction in accuracy when transfer is applied.

1) knowledge transfer is facilitated by the transfer of learned representations, 2) sparse coding can be used to learn transferable representations, and 3), alignment of the representations can be used to improve transfer even if the underlying representations are independently learned.
1) sparse coding representations are transferable between robots, and 2) Fisher vectors are not as transferable as sparse coding, even when the underlying representation is aligned.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how robots can learn object classifiers and then transfer the knowledge they have learned to another robot in a heterogeneous robot system.
how to best transfer object classifiers learned by one robot to another, with a specific emphasis on how to best transfer feature representations learned by one robot.
the problem of how robots can learn to recognize objects in a heterogeneous team and transfer this knowledge to other robots.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the transfer of sparse coding representations can indeed be successful in heterogeneous robot teams.

transfer of knowledge is indeed possible, and that the transfer is facilitated by the use of codebook methods, but that it is still possible to transfer knowledge effectively even if codebook methods are used.
knowledge transfer of learned object classifiers across heterogeneous robot teams is feasible and that alignment of the feature representations can help to improve the transfer.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the transfer of sparse coding representations is effective, but that the transfer of classifiers is not.

we show that knowledge transfer is possible in heterogeneous robot teams, even when using independently learned feature representations, and that it is possible to improve transfer performance by aligning the feature representations.

the transfer of knowledge from one robot to another can indeed be successful, but the success of transfer depends on several factors including the similarity of the underlying representations and the type of feature representation used.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of a common feature representation for both the training and testing robots can result in significant improvements in the ability to transfer knowledge across heterogeneous robots.
knowledge transfer is possible even when heterogeneous robots are involved and the underlying feature representations learned by each robot are different.
knowledge transfer in heterogeneous robot teams can be facilitated using the learned sparse feature representations themselves, without requiring the use of a codebook method.
